passages.t: ‘Let us make a name for ourselves’
passages.happening:
“Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech” (verse 1). People move east and settle on a plain in the land of Shinar (verse 2).

They say to one another, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly.” They use brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar (verse 3).

Then they go on: “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Shinar is the Bible's name for the land of Babylon, the flat plain of southern Mesopotamia between the Tigris and the Euphrates.

Verse 3 notes something a reader in Canaan would find strange. In Canaan people built with stone. Mesopotamia had little stone, so its builders made bricks of mud. For great buildings they baked the bricks hard in a kiln and set them with bitumen, a natural tar. The detail is true to the land, and it carries a hint of irony: people mean to reach heaven with bricks they have baked themselves.

The great cities of Mesopotamia had ziggurats: huge stepped towers of brick with a shrine at the top. Babylon's own ziggurat was called Etemenanki, ‘the house of the foundation of heaven and earth’. Many scholars think the tower of Babel story has towers like this in view.

Babylon's own creation poem, Enuma Elish, tells how the gods themselves made bricks and built Babylon and its great temple for their king, Marduk. Genesis tells the story of the same city very differently. Here it is built by proud people, and it is not the gate of heaven.

In the ancient world, kings ‘made a name’ by great buildings and conquests, and they carved their building works in stone so they would be remembered. The builders want two things: a name, and safety from being scattered. Both go against God's word. God had told Noah's family to “fill the earth” (9:1).
passages.later:
Babylon runs through the whole Bible as the city of human pride. Its armies took Judah into exile, and Daniel says the king carried the temple's treasures “to the land of Shinar” (Daniel 1:2). In Revelation a voice cries, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (Revelation 18:2).

The psalm gives the other way of building: “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).

In the very next chapter, God says to Abram, “I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). The builders tried to make a name. Abram receives one as a gift.
passages.asks: ‘Let us make a name for ourselves.’ Ask where you are trying to build a name: in work, in reputation, online. Then ask what you fear will happen if you do not. The builders feared being scattered. Ask what you are afraid of, and whether you have brought that fear to God.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building” (verse 5).

The LORD says that if, as one people with one language, they have begun to do this, “then nothing they devise will be beyond them” (verse 6). “Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another’s speech” (verse 7).

So the LORD scatters them over the face of all the earth, and they stop building the city (verse 8). “That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The story is full of irony. The builders mean their tower to reach the heavens. But God has to ‘come down’ to see it. From heaven, it is tiny.

They said ‘Come, let us build’. God answers, ‘Come, let Us go down’. Their words are turned back on them.

They built so that they would not be scattered. They are scattered.

And there is a play on words at the end. In the language of Babylon, the city's name was understood as Bab-ili, ‘the gate of the god’. In Hebrew, Babel sounds like balal, ‘to confuse’. Genesis takes the proud name and turns it into a joke: not the gate of God, but the place of confusion.

The first hearers may have lived in Babylon's shadow. Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and took its people away. To them, this story said: the city that looks so mighty is a place God came down to look at, and scattered.
passages.later:
Christians have long read the day of Pentecost as Babel turned around. When the Holy Spirit came, there were in Jerusalem people “from every nation under heaven” and “each one heard them speaking his own language” (Acts 2:5-6). At Babel one language was broken into many. At Pentecost the many languages are not erased; each one carries the same good news. The New Testament does not say it in so many words, but the echo is strong.

Zephaniah had looked for that day: “I will restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD” (Zephaniah 3:9).

Mary sings that God “has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts” (Luke 1:51). And James says, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).
passages.hard:
What exactly was the builders' sin? Readers have given several answers, and they fit together.

Pride. They wanted to make a name for themselves, apart from God.

Refusing God's command. God told people to fill the earth (9:1). The builders gathered in one place so they would not be scattered.

Reaching heaven on their own terms. A tower that ‘reaches to the heavens’ sounds like a temple tower, a way to climb up to God by human effort.

Power in one place. Some readers note that one city, one tower and one language can mean one power over everyone, the way empires work. God's scattering breaks that power.

Was God afraid of them? Verse 6 can sound that way. But the story itself undercuts it: God must come down even to see the tower. Most readers understand God's concern as care for people. A human race united in pride and cut off from God would multiply evil, as it did before the flood. So the scattering is both judgment and mercy. It stops the building, and it limits how far evil can spread.

Is this the origin of every language? Some read it so. Others note that chapter 10 already lists peoples ‘according to their languages’, and read chapter 11 as the story behind that list, told about Babylon in terms of the whole world. Christians differ on how to read it, and these notes do not settle it. On every reading, human pride cannot build its way to heaven.
passages.asks: God came down to see what the builders could not see about themselves. Ask what tower you are building, and whether it would look as small to God as theirs did. Then think of Pentecost. Ask whether you see people of other languages as a problem, or as part of the family God is gathering.

passages.happening:
A new section begins: “This is the account of Shem” (verse 10). Two years after the flood, Shem has a son, Arphaxad.

The list runs on like chapter 5: a father's age when his son is born, then the years he lived after. Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor (verses 12-25). But this time the list does not give each man's total age, and it does not say ‘and then he died’.

It ends with Terah: “When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
This list mirrors the one in chapter 5. That one ran ten generations from Adam to Noah and ended with a father of three sons. This one runs ten generations from Shem to Abram and ends the same way, with Terah and his three sons. A listener would feel the story narrowing toward one man.

Shem's name is the Hebrew word for ‘name’. Right after the builders try to make a name for themselves, the story turns to the family of ‘Name’, and through it to Abram, whose name God will make great.

Watch the ages fall. Shem lives 600 years in all. Peleg lives 239. Nahor lives 148. Human life is shrinking toward the lengths we know.

The numbers again differ between the ancient copies. The ancient Greek translation often adds years, and it adds one more name, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah. Luke's family line of Jesus follows the Greek here: “the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem” (Luke 3:36). Family lines were not always handed down exactly alike.
passages.later:
Luke traces Jesus' family back through every name in this list, from Abraham to Shem to Noah (Luke 3:34-36).

The point of the list is where it ends: with Abram. Paul says Scripture “foretold the gospel to Abraham” when God promised that all nations would be blessed through him (Galatians 3:8). The scattered nations of chapter 11 are the very ones that promise will reach.
passages.asks: The list narrows from the whole world to one family, and from that family to one man. Ask what it means that God works through ordinary families and long years of waiting. Then ask whose faithfulness, years before you, God used to bring you where you are.

passages.happening:
“This is the account of Terah.” Terah is the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran is the father of Lot (verse 27). Haran dies while his father is still living, in Ur of the Chaldeans (verse 28).

Abram marries Sarai, and Nahor marries Milcah, Haran's daughter (verse 29). Then a short sentence: “But Sarai was barren; she had no children” (verse 30).

Terah takes Abram, Sarai and his grandson Lot and sets out from Ur for the land of Canaan. But when they reach Haran, they settle there (verse 31). Terah dies in Haran at 205 (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Ur was an ancient and wealthy city in southern Mesopotamia. It was dug up between 1922 and 1934 by Leonard Woolley, for the British Museum and the Penn Museum. Its chief god was the moon god, Nanna, also called Sin. Haran, far to the north-west, was another city where the moon god was worshiped. Joshua later says that Terah's family “worshiped other gods” beyond the Euphrates (Joshua 24:2). Abram did not grow up worshiping the LORD.

The name ‘Ur of the Chaldeans’ uses the name of a people, the Chaldeans, who were settled in southern Babylonia by about 850 BC. Many scholars take the phrase as written or updated for later readers; others answer that an older name could have been brought up to date by a later scribe.

The family carries grief. One son, Haran, dies young, before his father. His son Lot travels with his grandfather.

Then verse 30 says the same thing twice: Sarai was barren; she had no children. In that world a childless marriage was a deep sorrow, and seemed to close off a family's future. The first hearers would feel the weight. And they would know what comes next: God is about to promise this childless couple that their family will become a great nation.
passages.later:
Stephen tells this story in Acts: “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran” (Acts 7:2). God says to Abram, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15:7). Hebrews says Abraham “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8), and that he was looking for “the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10). Babel's builders made their own city; Abraham waited for God's.

Sarai's barrenness begins a pattern in Scripture. Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 29:31) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2) all wait for children. In the New Testament Elizabeth is barren and old (Luke 1:7). Again and again God's promise comes through those who could not bring it about themselves.
passages.hard: A word of care. Sarai's story ends in joy, with a son, Isaac, in her old age. But that does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: The story of God's promise to Abram begins with a family that worshiped other gods, a son who died young and a wife who had no children. Ask what in your own story feels like a closed door. Then remember that this is where God chose to begin.
